analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit and disclose child labor anywhere in their supply chains, with fines up to $100 million.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Every US-listed company with more than $500 million in worldwide receipts would have to audit its entire supply chain each year for unlawful child labor, publish the results, and have its CEO certify under penalty of law that the findings are truthful. The Labor Department could fine companies up to $100 million for failing to report honestly, and up to $500 million for retaliating against workers who cooperate with auditors. The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, especially migrant teens, who would be less likely to be hired illegally to clean meat plants, pack boxes, or work overnight shifts for the country's largest companies and their contractors. Consumers and investors would also get a public, searchable record of which companies find child labor in their supply chains.

how_it_helps.text: Covered companies must audit their whole supply chain annually, including suppliers and on-site service providers like cleaning and food-service contractors, and interview workers off-site and confidentially so they can speak freely [S2].
Each company must publish its child-labor audit report on its website, with a conspicuous link from the homepage, so consumers can see the findings [S2].

The CEO must sign a certification that the company eradicated unlawful child labor and disclosed every known instance, with the federal False Statements Act applying to the report, making false claims a federal crime [S2].

The Secretary of Labor can assess civil damages up to $100 million against a company that violates the reporting requirements, and up to $500 million against any covered company, supplier, or contractor that willfully retaliates against a worker for participating in an audit [S2].
The bill bars retaliation against workers who cooperate with auditors and requires companies to write anti-retaliation protections into every supplier and service-provider contract [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with over $500 million in annual receipts would bear the cost of annual supply-chain audits, new compliance and record-keeping systems, public disclosure of violations, and potential fines in the tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. Suppliers and staffing or cleaning contractors would face new contract requirements and audit scrutiny.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with over $500 million in receipts

drawbacks.text: Annual full-supply-chain audits with confidential worker interviews, pay-stub collection, and dozens of mandatory document reviews are a heavy compliance burden, and the costs would likely be passed through to consumers in prices [S2].

The bill's remedy is disclosure, not a direct ban: a company can comply fully by reporting the child labor it finds, so whether violations actually decline depends on public pressure and the Labor Department choosing to enforce, and the bill gives the Secretary discretion rather than automatic penalties for the child labor itself [S2].
A $100 million fine cap may be small relative to the revenues of the largest covered companies, raising the risk that some firms would treat the fines as a cost of doing business [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: making large companies legally responsible for child labor buried in their supply chains, with public reporting and CEO-level criminal exposure, targets a problem that company self-policing has not solved. The costs are compliance-heavy but borne by the same companies that profit from the labor. The design's main weakness is that it relies on disclosure and discretionary enforcement rather than automatic penalties, so its effectiveness would depend on how vigorously the Labor Department used its new authority.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate's labor committee, and no one on the committee ever scheduled it for a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on May 3, 2023 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which was its final action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S4].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor during the two years the bill was pending [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations with large supply chains came out ahead, avoiding mandatory child-labor audits, public disclosure of violations, CEO certification, and fines of up to $100 million. Their suppliers and the staffing and cleaning contractors that place underage workers also avoided the new scrutiny.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Responsibility for Child Labor Elimination Act in the Senate on May 3, 2023.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where the bill sat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the referral to committee was the bill's final action for the entire Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: 41+ senators who could block committee and floor action; none cosponsored
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator signed on as a cosponsor to their own party member's bill, and the bill never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no one went on record in favor or against; the only measurable signals are a Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Large consumer-goods manufacturers and retailers (>$500M in receipts)
industries.note: The bill would have forced them to audit their supply chains for child labor, publish the findings, and expose their CEOs to federal false-statement liability, with fines up to $100 million. The bill's death left their existing self-policing in place.

The bill specifically covered 'on-site service providers' — the cleaning and staffing contractors through which underage workers have reached jobs at major facilities — and would have required anti-retaliation audit language in every contract. They avoided this scrutiny entirely.

Suppliers producing inputs for covered companies would have been subject to audits, worker interviews, and document reviews for child-labor compliance. The bill's failure removed this new layer of oversight.
